newsitem.title: USA: Licorice safe to eat, dangerous to smoke.
newsitem.headline: Licorice safe to eat, dangerous to smoke.

text.p: Licorice, honey and cocoa, all common foodstuffs, are also common cigarette flavorings and anti-smoking advocates said Friday that while those things are safe to eat, they are toxic when burned and inhaled.

"The oral route is fundamentally different from the inhaled route in terms of toxicity," Dr. David Burns of the University of California at San Diego told the Massachusetts Department of Public Health on the second day of public hearings.
The hearings are part of a process to design regulations that will require all companies that sell cigarettes and smokeless tobacco in Massachusetts to disclose the ingredients by brand by July 1.
The tobacco companies, which tried unsuccessfully to block the hearings from taking place, have so far submitted only a four-page statement saying the hearings are themselves illegal.

Four tobacco firms, Philip Morris Cos Inc., R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co., Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp. and Lorillard Tobacco Co. are suing in federal court to have the state law declared unconstitutional, arguing in part it would force them to reveal trade secrets.

During the hearing, several witnesses testified that flavorings used in foods, as well as, sweetners that are usually consumed on their own including licorice, honey and cocoa are carcinogens when burned and inhaled.

Speaking of licorice, John Pauly, a researcher at the Roswell Park Cancer Institute in Buffalo, N.Y., said, "You eat it. You ignite it. It gives rise to polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons. These are well known carcinogens."

Honey is number 273 on a list of 599 tobacco addictives that the industry released in 1994. University of California's Burns said, "It's well known when you burn sugar, you produce a wide range of products, but you produce carbon monoxide."
He said cocoa powder when used to flavor cigarettes develops a tobacco tar that is more carcinogenic.
